messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan was 39, a South Asian American interior designer living with his wife, and he described his life as having divided sharply into before and after the night his younger brother died without warning. Before that loss, he had been the sort of man who kept moving, always sketching ideas, visiting sites, choosing materials, and thinking ahead for clients. Afterward, the ordinary continuity of his days felt altered in ways he did not expect. He could still work, still come home, still speak to people, but there were moments when the world would suddenly narrow around the fact that his brother was gone, and in those moments he felt as if he were being pulled back into the worst part of it.

He spoke about the death as something that did not feel prepared for in any human sense. There had been no chance to say what he wanted to say, no gradual decline to brace himself against, only the abruptness of being told and then having to stand in the reality of it. In the first weeks afterward, funerals and any grief-related gathering felt unbearable to him. Even hearing other people talk about losing someone could leave him tense and watchful, as if the room had changed shape. He found himself avoiding memorials and anything that resembled one, and he also tried not to dwell on dates connected to the loss. As the anniversary approached each year, he would notice himself becoming more guarded, checking the calendar and then wishing he had not. He said he dreaded those days because they seemed to carry their own force, as though the date itself could bring everything back.

Over time, he became aware of how thoroughly he was trying to steer around reminders of death and loss. If a colleague mentioned a relative who had died, he would change the subject or step away. If a client meeting happened to touch on a family story or an event involving a bereavement, he would feel a sudden urge to leave the conversation. Even in his own home, he was careful about what he watched or listened to if it seemed likely to remind him of someone lost. He did not describe this as a dramatic choice so much as a practical one: he had come to believe that if he gave those reminders too much space, he might not be able to keep himself together.

Rohan also found himself mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios, especially when something about a day felt unsettled. He would imagine what might happen if another loved one were taken suddenly, or if an ordinary outing turned into another irretrievable moment. He did this, he said, in the hope that being prepared might make the future less shocking. Yet the rehearsals did not leave him calmer for long. They seemed to keep his attention fixed on loss, and he noticed that once a scenario started in his mind, it could be hard to put away.

At times, the past would arrive without warning. He described brief episodes in which he would suddenly feel as if he were back in that original shock, not merely remembering it but experiencing it with such force that his body seemed to know before his thinking did. He might be standing in a store or at his drafting table and then, for a few seconds, feel as though something terrible were happening again. Before he had time to reason with himself, his body would react as though danger were present. He found these moments especially frightening because they were so immediate, so physical, and so out of his control. Afterward, he would feel unsettled and irritated, tense with himself and with other people around him.

Those surges of irritability had become noticeable to him and, at times, to his wife. He described snapping more quickly than he used to, sounding harsher than he intended, and then feeling embarrassed afterward. At work, where his role required patience, precision, and collaboration, this was difficult to hide. He could still do the technical parts of his job, but he noticed that on days when grief reminders were nearby or an anniversary was approaching, he was less tolerant of interruptions and more easily angered by small frustrations. The strain of holding himself together often showed up in the spaces between tasks, when he was alone long enough to realize how keyed up he felt.

By the time he came for help, Rohan was tired of structuring his life around avoiding reminders and bracing for dates he could not stop from arriving. He did not want to keep carrying the sense that loss could come back at him in an instant, nor did he want his wife and work to keep absorbing the aftereffects of his reactions. What brought him in now was a growing fear that he was living too narrowly, always scanning for what might remind him, always half-preparing for the next blow. He hoped that treatment might help him feel less hijacked by those moments and allow him to face the anniversary, the grief talk, and the unexpected surges of memory without feeling as though he had been thrown back into the night his brother died.
